[[Category:Proper name]]
The '''Hubble parameter''', denoted by $H(t)$, describes the rate of the [[cosmic expansion]] in the [[standard cosmology model]] at any given instance in the [[Universe]]'s history.

== Formal definition ==

In the [[standard cosmology model]],

$$
H(t)\equiv \frac{\dot{a}(t)}{a(t)},
$$

<blockquote>
This definition is consistent with the experimental obversations of [[Person:Edwin Hubble|Edwin Hubble]] described in [[Hubble-Lemaître law]].

{{Hidden proof}}

Let $l$ denote physical distance, $c$ speed of light, $t$ time.

Since Newtonian approximations are valid below [[the cosmological scale]]:

$$
dl \simeq c\,dt \Rightarrow  dt=\frac{dl}{c} \tag{1}
$$

By [[redshift#Relativistic_description|the relativistic description of redshift]],

{{#content:Q2609|noPreNote}}

Let the present time be $t_o$.

For a nearby galaxy within [[the cosmological scale]], $t_e=t_o-dt$

Hence,

$$
z=\frac{a(t_o)}{a(t_o-dt)}-1=\frac{1}{1-\frac{\dot{a}(t_0)}{a(t_0)}dt}-1=\frac{\dot{a}(t_0)}{a(t_0)}dt \tag{2}
$$

Combine 1,2

$$
z=\frac{\dot{a}(t_0)}{a(t_0)}\frac{dl}{c} \tag{2}
$$

Recall the non-relativistic [[Doppler effect]] approximation of redshift

{{#content:Q2611|noPreNote}}

$$
\therefore \frac{v_r}{c} = \frac{\dot{a}(t_0)}{a(t_0)}\frac{dl}{c} \\
\therefore v_r=\frac{\dot{a}(t_0)}{a(t_0)}\,dl
\therefore v_r=H\,dl
$$

{{End hidden}}
</blockquote>

== Modern day value $H_0$ ==

The value of $H(t_0)$, where $t_0$ is the current [[cosmic time]], often denoted simply by $H_0$, is approximately 

$$
70 \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}
$$

where $\mathrm{Mpc}$ denotes megaparsec ( $10^6$ [[parsec]]s).
